chapters.name: Chapter 1: The job, the hardware and the network

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The help-desk job and the two A+ exams
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: List the two A+ exams, their codes and the main topics each one covers.
This lesson builds toward: Using the official CompTIA A+ exam pages, you will write a study and test plan with target dates for Core 1 and Core 2, covering every exam domain with its weight and a weekly study time.
A support technician answers calls, chats and tickets, sets up computers and accounts, fixes common problems, and knows when to pass a hard problem to a senior tech. Job titles include help desk technician, IT support specialist, desktop support and field technician.
CompTIA A+ is a well-known entry certification for this work. It is granted by CompTIA, not by this course. You must pass two exams. Core 1 (220-1201) covers mobile devices, networking, hardware, virtualization and cloud, and hardware and network troubleshooting. Core 2 (220-1202) covers operating systems, security, software troubleshooting and operational procedures. You can take them in either order.
When we checked in October 2026, each exam had up to 90 questions in 90 minutes, with multiple-choice, drag-and-drop and performance-based questions (small hands-on tasks). CompTIA recommends about 12 months of hands-on experience, but this is a recommendation. Exams, prices and versions change, so always check the official pages before you book.
Each exam lists domains (topic areas) with a weight, the share of the exam that topic makes up. Your study time should follow those weights.
Step by step:
- Open the official CompTIA A+ page.
- Open the Core 1 and Core 2 exam pages.
- Write down each exam code and its domains with their weights.
- Find the current price and testing options (test center or online) on the official site.
Words to know:
- Help desk: the team people contact when their technology does not work.
- Certification: a credential you earn by passing an exam, showing you have certain skills.
- Domain: a topic area of an exam. Its weight is the share of questions about it.
- Performance-based question: an exam task where you do something, like match settings or fix a setup, instead of picking one answer.
Official sources:
- CompTIA A+ certification (official page)
- CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1201) exam details
- CompTIA A+ Core 2 (220-1202) exam details
- US Bureau of Labor Statistics: Computer Support Specialists
Try it now: Open the official Core 1 and Core 2 pages. On paper, make two columns, one per exam. Write the exam code, then each domain and its weight. Circle the biggest domain in each exam: that is where you will spend the most study time.
You can now name the two A+ exams, their codes and their main domains, and find the current details on the official page.

check.q: How many exams must you pass to earn CompTIA A+?
check.why: A+ needs both Core 1 and Core 2; the course only prepares you.

check.q: Where should you check the current A+ price and exam version?
options: A forum post from last year
check.why: Prices and exam versions change; the official page is the only reliable source.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Inside the computer: the main hardware parts
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Identify the main hardware parts of a computer and say what each one does.
This lesson builds toward: Given pictures or a list of computer parts, you will identify each main hardware part and say what it does, getting at least 8 of 10 right.
Hardware is the physical parts you can touch. The motherboard is the main board everything plugs into. The CPU (processor) does the thinking. RAM (memory) holds what you are working on right now and is cleared when the power goes off. Storage keeps your files when the power is off: an SSD (solid-state drive, fast, no moving parts) or an HDD (hard disk drive, slower, spinning disks).
The power supply (PSU) turns wall power into the power the parts use. A graphics card (GPU) draws the picture on the screen; many computers have graphics built into the CPU. Ports on the outside include USB (USB-A and the smaller, reversible USB-C), HDMI and DisplayPort for screens, and Ethernet for a wired network.
A common help-desk clue: a slow computer that has many programs open may need more RAM; a computer that takes a long time to start may have a nearly full or older hard drive.
Safety first: you do not need to open a computer for this course. A technician always turns the computer off and unplugs it before opening it, wears an anti-static wrist strap, and never opens a power supply or a swollen battery.
Words to know:
- Hardware: the physical parts of a computer.
- CPU: the processor; the part that runs programs and does calculations.
- RAM: short-term memory that holds open programs and files; it empties when the power is off.
- SSD / HDD: storage drives that keep files when the power is off. An SSD is faster and has no moving parts.
- Motherboard: the main circuit board that connects all the parts.
- ESD: electrostatic discharge: a small static shock that can damage computer parts.
Try it now: Look at your own computer from the outside only. List every port you can see and name it (USB-A, USB-C, HDMI, Ethernet, headphone). Then, on Windows open Settings > System > About, or on a Mac open the Apple menu > About This Mac, and write down your processor and how much RAM (memory) the computer has.
You can now name the main parts of a computer, say what each does, and find your own computer's processor and memory.

check.q: Which part keeps your files when the computer is turned off?
check.why: Storage (SSD or HDD) keeps files; RAM empties when the power goes off.

check.q: Before opening a desktop computer, what does a technician do first?
options: Turn it off and unplug it
Remove the battery while it runs
check.why: Power off and unplug first; this protects you and the parts.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Networking basics: IP addresses, ipconfig and ping
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Check a computer's network connection with ipconfig and ping and record the results.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own Windows or Mac computer, you will run ipconfig (or check network settings) and ping to record the IP address and default gateway and test the connection, without help, and say what a 169.254 address means.
Every device on a network gets an IP address, like a street address for data. At home it usually looks like 192.168.x.x or 10.x.x.x. Your router hands out these addresses automatically with a service called DHCP. The default gateway is the router's address: the door from your home network to the internet.
If a Windows computer shows an address starting with 169.254, it could not get an address from DHCP. That is a big clue: check the cable or Wi-Fi, then the router.
Two tools every tech uses: ipconfig shows your IP address and default gateway (on Windows, open Command Prompt and type ipconfig). ping sends a small test message to another device and shows whether it answers. Ping the default gateway first; if that works, ping a website such as comptia.org.
Practice these only on your own computer and network. Some library or work computers block the command prompt; if so, use network settings to find your IP address instead.
Step by step:
- Windows: press the Windows key, type cmd and open Command Prompt. Mac: open Terminal.
- Windows: type ipconfig and press Enter. Write down the IPv4 address and the default gateway. Mac: find the IP address and router in System Settings > Network.
- Type ping followed by your gateway address, for example ping 192.168.1.1, and press Enter.
- On a Mac, press Control and C to stop ping.
- Read the result: replies mean the connection works; "timed out" or "unreachable" means it does not.
Words to know:
- IP address: a number that identifies a device on a network.
- DHCP: the service, usually in the router, that gives devices their IP addresses automatically.
- Default gateway: the router's address; the way out from your network to the internet.
- ipconfig: a Windows command that shows your network settings.
- ping: a command that tests whether another device answers over the network.
- Router: the box that connects your home network to the internet.
Official sources:
- CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1201) exam details
Try it now: On your own computer, follow the steps. Write down your IP address and default gateway, then ping the gateway and ping comptia.org. Write "works" or "does not work" for each. Keep this note for your final task.
You can now find your IP address and default gateway, test a connection with ping, and say what a 169.254 address means.

check.q: A Windows laptop shows the IP address 169.254.20.5. What does this tell you?
options: It did not get an address from DHCP
check.why: A 169.254 address means the device could not reach DHCP, so check the connection and router.

check.q: Which command shows a Windows computer's IP address and default gateway?
check.why: ipconfig shows your network settings; ping tests a connection.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Systems, troubleshooting and your plan

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Operating system tools you use every day
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find the system version, free storage, running programs and update status on your own computer.
This lesson builds toward: Using your own computer, you will find the operating system version, free storage, running programs and update status with built-in tools, in under 10 minutes.
The operating system (OS) is the main program that runs the computer: Windows, macOS, Linux, or on phones Android and iOS. A+ Core 2 expects you to find your way around these.
On Windows: Settings > System > About shows the version. Settings > System > Storage shows free space. Task Manager (press Ctrl + Shift + Esc) shows running programs and how hard the CPU and memory are working; you can end a frozen program there. Settings > Windows Update shows whether updates are waiting.
On a Mac: the Apple menu > About This Mac shows the version. Activity Monitor (search for it with Spotlight) shows running programs. System Settings > General > Software Update shows updates. Storage is under System Settings > General > Storage.
Good security habits are part of the job: install updates, keep the built-in antivirus on (Microsoft Defender on Windows), use a standard (non-admin) account for daily work, and lock the screen when you step away (Windows key + L on Windows).
Step by step:
- Find the OS name and version.
- Find how much storage is free.
- Open Task Manager or Activity Monitor and find the program using the most memory.
- Check for updates.
- Lock your screen, then unlock it.
Words to know:
- Operating system (OS): the main software that runs a computer or phone, like Windows or macOS.
- Task Manager: a Windows tool that shows running programs and lets you close a frozen one.
- Activity Monitor: the Mac tool that shows running programs.
- Admin account: an account that can install software and change settings. Daily work should use a standard account.
Official sources:
- CompTIA A+ Core 2 (220-1202) exam details
Try it now: On your own computer, write down: the OS name and version, free storage, the program using the most memory right now, and whether any updates are waiting. Add this to your network note from Lesson 3. You now have most of part 2 of your final task.
You can now use built-in tools to check a computer's version, storage, running programs and updates.

check.q: A program is frozen on Windows. Which tool lets you close it?
check.why: Task Manager shows running programs and can end one that is frozen.

check.q: Which is the safer habit for everyday work?
options: Using a standard account and keeping updates on
Turning off the antivirus to save speed
check.why: A standard account and current updates limit the damage if something goes wrong.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: The six-step troubleshooting method
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Apply the six CompTIA troubleshooting steps to a problem, in order.
This lesson builds toward: Given a computer problem from a user, you will apply the six-step CompTIA troubleshooting method and write down each step, with all six steps in the right order.
Good techs do not guess. They follow a method. The A+ objectives use six steps: 1. Identify the problem. 2. Establish a theory of probable cause (question the obvious). 3. Test the theory to find the cause. 4. Make a plan of action and carry out the fix. 5. Verify the whole system works and, if it helps, take steps to stop it happening again. 6. Document what you found, what you did and the result.
Step 1 means asking the user questions: What happened? When did it start? Did anything change? Is there an error message? Back up important data before you change anything.
Step 2 means starting with the simple causes: Is it plugged in? Is Wi-Fi on? Has it been restarted? If your first theory is wrong, make a new one and test again, or escalate (pass it to a senior tech).
Example: a printer will not print. Theory: it is offline. Test: the printer screen shows a paper jam. Fix: clear the jam safely. Verify: print a test page. Document: "Paper jam in tray 2, cleared, test page printed."
Step by step:
- Identify the problem: ask questions, back up data.
- Establish a theory of probable cause: start with the obvious.
- Test the theory. Wrong? Make a new theory or escalate.
- Make a plan and carry out the fix.
- Verify it works and prevent a repeat if you can.
- Document findings, actions and outcome.
Words to know:
- Troubleshooting: finding and fixing the cause of a problem step by step.
- Theory of probable cause: your best guess at what is causing the problem.
- Escalate: pass a problem to someone with more skill or access.
- Document: write down what you found and did, usually in the ticket.
Official sources:
- CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1201) exam details
Try it now: Pick a real problem you have had (slow laptop, no Wi-Fi, a phone that will not charge) or use: "A user cannot connect to Wi-Fi after moving desks." Write all six steps for it on paper, with what you would ask, check and write down at each step.
You can now work through a problem with the six troubleshooting steps and write each one down.

check.q: What is the FIRST troubleshooting step?
check.why: You must understand the problem before you guess at a cause.

check.q: You fixed the problem. What comes before documenting it?
options: Close the ticket without telling the user
Back up data for the first time
check.why: Step 5 is to verify everything works; step 6 is to document.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Tickets, talking to users, and your A+ study plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a complete help-desk ticket and a dated A+ study and test plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given a call or message from a user with a problem, you will write a help-desk ticket and a short, polite reply to the user, with every ticket field filled in and no blame or jargon in the reply. Using the official CompTIA A+ exam pages, you will write a study and test plan with target dates for Core 1 and Core 2, covering every exam domain with its weight and a weekly study time.
A ticket is the record of one problem. A good ticket has: the user's name and how to reach them (in a real job, from the company system), the device, a short summary, the details and any error message, the priority (how urgent), the steps taken, and the result. Write it so another tech could pick it up and understand it.
How you talk matters as much as the fix. Listen without interrupting, repeat the problem back, use plain words, never blame the user, give a time when you will update them, and confirm with them that it is fixed before you close the ticket. Keep their information private.
Now plan your exams. Use the domain weights you wrote in Lesson 1. Pick a target date for each exam. Spend more weeks on the bigger domains. Use free practice: CompTIA's free exam objectives document, your own computer, and the knowledge checks here. Many people study 5 to 10 hours a week; choose what fits your life and write it down.
Before you book, check the official page for the current price, any discount programs and testing options. Workforce centers, veterans programs and reentry programs sometimes help with exam costs, so ask yours.
Step by step:
- Ticket: fill in user, device, summary, details, priority, steps taken and result.
- Reply: thank them, say what you found in plain words, say what happens next and when.
- Plan: write a target date for Core 1 and Core 2.
- List each domain with its weight and the weeks you give it.
- Write your weekly study hours and where you will study.
- Check the official page for price and testing options; ask a local program about help with costs.
Words to know:
- Ticket: the written record of one support request, from start to finish.
- Priority: how urgent a ticket is, often low, medium, high or critical.
- Study plan: a written schedule of what you will study, when, and your exam date.
Official sources:
- CompTIA A+ certification (official page)
- CompTIA A+ Core 1 (220-1201) exam details
- CompTIA A+ Core 2 (220-1202) exam details
Try it now: Final task: write the ticket for your Lesson 5 problem with every field and the six steps, plus a two-sentence reply to the user. Put your computer note from Lessons 3 and 4 on one page. Then write your A+ study and test plan: target dates for Core 1 and Core 2, each domain and its weight, and your weekly hours.
You can now write a clear support ticket, reply to a user politely, and follow your own dated plan toward both A+ exams.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Computer note Missing the OS version, free storage or updates. Lists OS and version, free storage, the top memory user and update status. Also lists the processor and RAM and says what they mean for speed. Network check No IP address or gateway, or ping not tried. Records IP address and gateway and the result of pinging both the gateway and a website. Explains what the results would mean if one ping failed, including a 169.254 address. Troubleshooting steps Steps missing or out of order, or the fix is a guess. All six steps in order, with what was asked, tested and done. Includes a second theory or an escalation point and a way to stop it happening again. Ticket and reply Ticket is vague or the reply blames the user or uses jargon. Every ticket field is filled in; the reply is polite, plain and says what happens next. Another person could follow the ticket without asking any questions. Study and test plan No dates, or domains are missing. Target dates for Core 1 and Core 2, every domain with its weight, weekly hours. Plan gives more weeks to heavier domains and names where to check price and get help with costs. Hardware words Hardware parts are named wrongly in the note or ticket. Parts and ports are named correctly. Links a symptom to a likely part, for example slow with many programs open and low RAM. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which ticket summary is most useful?
options: "Laptop cannot connect to office Wi-Fi since moving to desk 14; error: no internet."
check.why: It names the device, the problem, when it started and the error, with no blame.

check.q: Core 1 has a domain worth 28% and one worth 11%. How should you plan?
options: Give more study time to the 28% domain
check.why: Bigger weights mean more questions, so they deserve more study time.
